title: Earn, Save, Spend, Share
bigQuestion: How does money you earn today turn into something you want later?

story.title: One Lawn at a Time
story.kicker: The bike in the window cost $120. Mateo had $6 and a lawn mower he was allowed to borrow.
paragraphs: The bike hung in the shop window all spring. It was blue with a black seat. The tag said $120. Mateo walked past it every day on the way home from school. He had $6 in a sock in his drawer. He also had a neighbor, Mrs. Ortiz, whose grass was getting tall.

"I could mow it," Mateo told his mom. "For money." His mom thought about it. "You can use our mower if I am there the first few times," she said. "Ten dollars a lawn is fair for a small yard. But you have to finish every job you start. Edges, too. And you put the mower back clean." Mateo said yes to all of it.

The first Saturday he mowed Mrs. Ortiz's yard. It took an hour and he was sweaty and tired. She handed him a ten-dollar bill. He held it for a long time. Then he did the math. Ten dollars a lawn. One hundred twenty dollars. "Twelve lawns," he said. "That is a lot of lawns."

His mom got out an empty jar. She taped a picture of the blue bike to the front. "Every lawn, the money goes in here," she said. "Not in the sock. Not in your pocket. In the jar, where you can see it." Mateo dropped in the ten and the six from his sock. Sixteen dollars. The jar looked very empty.

By June, two more neighbors had hired him. Some weeks he wanted to spend a ten on a game with his friends. Most weeks he did not. He put a mark on the calendar each time he mowed. In July, the jar held $120. He walked to the shop with his mom and a jar of small bills. The bike was still there.
story.think: What made it hard for Mateo to keep saving? What helped him? Why did his mom want the money in a jar, not in his pocket?

lessons.title: Ways Kids Earn
lessons.mainIdea: People earn money by doing work that someone else needs done, and the work comes first.
reading: Picture a Saturday morning. One kid is walking a neighbor's dog. Another is pulling weeds for a grandparent. A third is selling lemonade on the corner. Each one is *earning* money. To earn means to get money in return for work. The work comes first. The money comes after.

Kids earn in many ways. Mowing a lawn, raking leaves, shoveling snow, washing a car, watching a younger cousin while a parent is in the next room. Some families pay for extra chores. Some do not, and that is fair too. Regular chores are part of being in a family. Extra work for a neighbor is a job.

A job has rules. Agree on the pay before you start. Show up when you said you would. Finish the whole job, not most of it. Put the tools back. A kid who does all four gets asked back. That is how one lawn turns into three. Always ask a grown-up before you take a job for someone outside the family.

words.d: to get money in return for work you do
work you agree to do for someone, usually for pay

look.title: The Half-Done Lawn
look.text: Jada agreed to mow Mr. Lee's lawn for $10. She mowed the front yard, got hot, and went home. She left the mower in the driveway. The next day she asked Mr. Lee for the $10.
look.prompt: Which of the job rules did Jada break? What should she do now, and what might happen the next time she asks for work?

check.q: What does it mean to earn money?
choices: To find money on the ground
To get money in return for work
To get money as a gift
To borrow money from a friend
check.why: Earning means doing work first and being paid for it after.

check.q: When should you agree on the pay for a job?
check.why: Agreeing on pay before you start stops arguments and surprises later.

check.q: Why does a kid who finishes the whole job get asked back?
choices: Because they used their own tools
Because people can count on them
check.why: Finishing every job and putting tools back makes you someone people trust with more work.

lessons.title: Counting What You Earned
lessons.mainIdea: Write down every job and every dollar, and subtract what the job cost you, so you know what you really made.
reading: Mateo mows three lawns in one week at $10 each. How much did he earn? 3 times 10 is $30. But he also bought a box of lawn bags for $4 to hold the clippings. The bags were an *expense*, a cost of doing the job. What he kept is $30 minus $4, or $26.

Keep a *record*. A record is a written list of what happened. Draw four columns on a page: date, job, money in, money out. Every time you get paid, write it down. Every time you spend on the job, write that too. At the end of the week, add each column. The difference is what you really made.

A record catches mistakes. Without one, kids often think they earned more than they did. "I mowed a lot" feels like $50 but might be $30. And a record shows a neighbor you are serious. A common mistake is writing the pay down only when you feel like it. Write it every single time.

words.d: money you spend to do a job or to live, like lawn bags or a bus fare
a written list of money that came in and money that went out

look.title: Mateo's Lawn Money, Four Weeks (example)
look.prompt: How much did Mateo earn in four weeks? If he spent $4 on lawn bags in week 3, how much did he keep in all?

check.q: Three lawns at $10 each, minus $4 for bags. What did Mateo keep?
check.why: 3 times 10 is 30, and 30 minus 4 is 26.

check.q: What is an expense?
choices: Money you spend to do a job
check.why: An expense is a cost, like the lawn bags, that comes out of what you earned.

check.q: What should go in a money record?
choices: Every dollar in and every dollar out
check.why: A full record of money in and money out shows what you really made.

lessons.title: A Want Now or a Goal Later
lessons.mainIdea: Every dollar spent on a small want today is a dollar that cannot go toward a bigger goal later.
reading: Mateo has a ten-dollar bill in his hand. His friends are going for pizza and a game. It would cost about $8. He could go. He would have fun. But his *goal* is a $120 bike. A goal is something you decide to work toward. Every ten he spends is a lawn that did not count.

This is the hardest part of money. A want now feels big. A goal later feels far away. Both are real. Nobody has to say no to every small thing. But you have to choose on purpose. Ask: if I spend this, how much longer until my goal? For Mateo, one $8 pizza night is almost one whole lawn.

One trick helps. Look at the picture on the jar before you decide. Another trick is to give yourself a small spending amount each week, and no more. When it is gone, it is gone. Then a pizza night is planned, not stolen from the bike. The goal keeps moving forward.

words.d: something you decide to work toward, like saving $120 for a bike
picking one thing when you cannot have both

look.title: Ten Dollars, Two Doors
look.text: Behind door one: pizza and a game with friends tonight, $8. Behind door two: the same $8 goes in the bike jar, and the bike is $8 closer. Mateo has $60 in the jar and needs $120. Friends are waiting.
look.prompt: What would you do, and why? Is there a way to do some of both over the summer?

check.q: What is a goal?
choices: A thing you want right now
Something you decide to work toward
check.why: A goal is a target you choose and work toward over time.

check.q: Mateo spends $8 on pizza. How does that change his bike goal?
choices: It puts the bike about one lawn further away
It does not change the goal
It doubles the time to the goal
check.why: At $10 a lawn, $8 spent is most of one lawn's pay that did not go in the jar.

check.q: What is a good way to enjoy some wants and still reach a goal?
choices: Borrow from the jar and pay it back later
Set a small weekly spending amount and stop when it is gone
check.why: A planned spending amount lets you have fun without taking from the goal.

lessons.title: The Jar With a Picture
lessons.mainIdea: Saving works best when the money has one place to go and you can see the goal every day.
reading: To *save* means to keep money instead of spending it, so you can use it later. The simplest tool is a jar. Take a clear jar. Tape a picture of your goal on it. Write the goal amount on the tape: "$120." Put the jar where you will see it every day.

Why a jar and not a pocket? Money in a pocket gets spent. Money in a sock gets forgotten. Money in a clear jar with a picture on it has a job, and you can watch it grow. Every time you put money in, count it and write the new total on a card next to the jar.

Some families use an envelope, a box or a savings account instead. Any of these work. What matters is the same. One place. A picture or a name for the goal. A total you update. The mistake to avoid is "borrowing" from the jar. Once you start taking money out, the jar stops working.

words.d: to keep money instead of spending it, so you can use it later
the money you have saved up so far

look.title: Three Ways to Keep Money
look.text: Kid A keeps money loose in a coat pocket. Kid B keeps it in a sock in a drawer. Kid C keeps it in a clear jar with a picture of a skateboard on it and a card that says $38 so far.
look.prompt: Which kid will most likely reach a goal, and why? What could go wrong for the other two?

check.q: What does it mean to save money?
choices: To keep it so you can use it later
To spend it on a need
To hide it and forget it
check.why: Saving is keeping money out of spending so it can reach a goal.

check.q: Why tape a picture of the goal on the jar?
choices: It reminds you what the money is for
check.why: Seeing the goal every day makes it easier to leave the money alone.

check.q: What makes a savings jar stop working?
choices: Putting in coins instead of bills
Writing the total on a card
Keeping it where you can see it
Taking money out for small wants
check.why: Borrowing from the jar undoes the saving and slows the goal.

lessons.title: How Long Until the Goal
lessons.mainIdea: Divide the goal by what you save each week to see how many weeks it will take.
reading: A goal needs a number and a date. Mateo's bike is $120. He earns about $30 a week from lawns. He decides to save $20 of it each week and keep $10 for spending. How many weeks until the bike? Divide the goal by the weekly savings. 120 divided by 20 is 6. Six weeks.

Now try it another way. If he saves all $30, then 120 divided by 30 is 4 weeks. If he saves only $10, then 120 divided by 10 is 12 weeks. The more you save each week, the sooner you get there. But the plan has to be one you can really keep. A plan you quit is slower than a smaller plan you finish.

Make a chart. Down the side, write the weeks. Next to each week, write the total in the jar. Week 1, $20. Week 2, $40. Week 3, $60. When you can see the finish line, it is easier to keep going. If a week goes wrong and you save less, do not quit. Just add one more week to the chart.

words.d: happening once each week
the whole amount when everything is added together

look.title: The Bike Jar, $20 a Week (example)
look.prompt: In which week does Mateo reach $120? What would the chart look like if he saved $30 a week instead?

check.q: The goal is $120. You save $20 a week. How many weeks?
check.why: 120 divided by 20 is 6 weeks.

check.q: The goal is $120. You save $30 a week. How many weeks?
check.why: 120 divided by 30 is 4 weeks.

check.q: You planned to save $20 but one week you could only save $10. What should you do?
choices: Keep going and add a week
check.why: A slow week only adds a little time; quitting adds all of it.

lessons.title: What a Bank Does
lessons.mainIdea: A bank keeps money safe, keeps a record of it, and lets you take it out when you need it.
reading: A jar works for $120. It does not work for $1,000. Money in a jar can be lost, stolen or burned in a fire. A *bank* is a business that keeps money safe. When you put money in, the bank writes it down in your *account*. An account is the bank's record of your money.

Putting money in is called a *deposit*. Taking money out is called a withdrawal. The bank sends a statement, a list of every deposit and withdrawal, so you can check it against your own record. Kids can often open a savings account with a parent or guardian on it. Ask a grown-up at home.

The money in a bank is not sitting in a box with your name on it. The bank keeps careful records instead. That is why the statement matters. Read it. If a number looks wrong, tell a grown-up. And never share your account numbers with anyone outside your family.

words.d: a business that keeps money safe and keeps records of it
the bank's record of your money, with every deposit and withdrawal
money you put into a bank account

look.title: Reading a Statement
look.text: Ana's savings statement says: opening balance $50.00; deposit $20.00; deposit $20.00; withdrawal $15.00; closing balance $75.00. Ana's own record says she deposited $20 twice and took out $15 once.
look.prompt: Does the bank's math match Ana's record? Add it up. What should Ana do if it did not match?

check.q: What is a deposit?
choices: Money you put into an account
Money you take out of an account
Money the bank keeps for itself
check.why: A deposit is money going in; a withdrawal is money coming out.

check.q: Ana starts with $50, deposits $20 twice and withdraws $15. What is her balance?
Why is a bank safer than a jar for a large amount?
choices: Banks keep records and money cannot be lost in a fire at home
Banks give you a bigger jar
Money in a bank cannot be withdrawn
check.why: A bank keeps money safe and keeps a written record of every dollar.

lessons.title: Interest, Money for Saving
lessons.mainIdea: A bank pays interest, a small amount added to your savings for leaving the money there.
reading: Here is something a jar cannot do. A bank pays you for keeping your money there. That payment is called *interest*. Interest is extra money added to your account because you saved. The bank uses the money you deposit to make loans, and it shares a little of what it earns with you.

Interest is figured as a *percent* of what you saved. Percent means "out of one hundred." Here is an example with easy numbers. You put $100 in a savings account. The bank pays 2 percent interest for the year. Two percent of $100 is $2. At the end of the year you have $102. You did nothing but leave it alone.

Real interest rates change and are often smaller or larger than this example. The idea is what matters. Saving in a bank makes money grow a little on its own. The longer it sits, the more it earns. The mistake is expecting it to grow fast. Interest is slow and steady. Lawns are faster. Both together are best.

words.d: money a bank adds to your savings for keeping your money there
out of one hundred; 2 percent of $100 is $2

look.title: $100 Saved at 2 Percent a Year (example)
look.cite: Example with simple rounded numbers; real rates differ
look.prompt: How much interest did the account earn each year? What would happen to the numbers if you also deposited $20 every month?

check.q: What is interest?
choices: A fee you pay the bank
The picture on a savings jar
Money the bank adds to your savings
Money you earn from a job
check.why: Interest is what a bank pays you for keeping your money with it.

check.q: You save $100 at 2 percent for one year. How much interest do you earn?
check.why: Two percent of $100 is $2, so the account grows to $102.

check.q: Which describes interest best?
check.why: Interest grows savings a little at a time, so it works best over a long time.

lessons.title: Spend, Save, Share
lessons.mainIdea: Splitting every dollar that comes in into spend, save and share gives each part of your money a job.
reading: Picture three jars on a shelf. One says spend. One says save. One says share. When money comes in, it gets split three ways before any of it is used. Some for now, some for later, some for others. This is the simplest money plan there is, and many grown-ups still use it.

Try it with a $10 allowance. Put $5 in spend. Put $3 in save. Put $2 in share. That is one way. Another family might do $4, $4 and $2. There is no single right split. The rule is that all three jars get something every time. Spend is for small wants now. Save is for the goal. Share is for helping someone else.

The mistake most kids make is filling spend first and saving what is left. Usually nothing is left. Fill save first, then share, then spend. A person who can split $10 three ways can later split a paycheck three ways. The habit is the whole point.

words.d: money some families give a child on a regular schedule, like once a week
to give part of what you have to help someone else

look.title: Split the Ten
look.text: Three jars: spend, save, share. You just got $10. Your goal is a $40 art set. You also want to help with the class food drive. And there is a $3 comic book you like.
look.prompt: How would you split the $10 across the three jars? Show that your three amounts add to $10, and say why you chose them.

check.q: What are the three jars for?
check.why: Spend is for now, save is for the goal, share is for helping others.

check.q: $10 comes in. Spend gets $5 and save gets $3. How much goes to share?
check.why: 5 + 3 = 8, and 10 minus 8 leaves $2 for share.

check.q: What is the mistake of filling the spend jar first?
choices: The spend jar gets too heavy
The bank will not accept it
There is usually nothing left to save
check.why: Saving what is left after spending usually means saving nothing; fill save first.

lessons.title: A Budget From an Allowance
lessons.mainIdea: A budget is a written plan that gives every dollar coming in a place to go, and the parts must add up to the total.
reading: A *budget* is a plan for money, written down before you spend it. It has two sides. Money in and money out. Money in is your *income*, what you earn or receive. Money out is where each dollar goes. The rule is simple. The money out must add up to exactly the money in. Not more.

Here is a weekly example. Income: $10 allowance plus $10 from one lawn is $20. Money out: save $8, share $2, snacks $4, bus fare to the library $3, spending money $3. Add the money out: 8 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 20. It matches. Every dollar has a job. Nothing is missing and nothing is extra.

At the end of the week, compare the plan to what really happened. If snacks cost $6 instead of $4, something else got $2 less. That is normal. Fix the plan for next week. A budget is not a punishment. It is a map that shows where the money went, so you can steer it where you want.

words.d: a written plan that gives every dollar coming in a place to go
the money that comes in, from work, allowance or gifts
when money out adds up to exactly money in, with nothing missing or extra

look.title: A Weekly Budget for $20 (example)
look.prompt: Add the five rows. Do they equal the $20 income? If snacks went up to $6, which row would you cut, and why?

check.q: What is a budget?
choices: A written plan for where money will go
A list of things you want
check.why: A budget plans each dollar before it is spent.

check.q: Income is $20. Save $8, share $2, snacks $4, bus $3. How much is left for spending money?
What should the money out add up to?
check.why: In a balanced budget, money out equals money in, so every dollar has a job.

lessons.title: Giving to Others
lessons.mainIdea: Sharing money, things or time with others is part of a healthy money plan, and even a small gift counts.
reading: The share jar is the smallest, but it may matter the most. Sharing means giving part of what you have to help someone else. It can be money. It can be things, like a coat that no longer fits. It can be time, like helping at a food drive. All three are real ways to give.

Many families give to a place of worship, a food pantry, an animal shelter or a neighbor who is having a hard time. Kids can give too. A can of soup for the class food drive. Two dollars from the share jar for a school fundraiser. Sorting cans at a pantry with a grown-up. None of it has to be big.

Give carefully. Ask a grown-up before you give money to anyone, especially online or to a stranger who calls. Real groups will never rush you. Then notice how you feel after you give. Most people feel richer, not poorer. That feeling is why the share jar exists.

words.d: a place that gives free food to people who need it
to give money, things or time to a group that helps others

look.title: Three Ways to Give
look.text: Kim has $2 in her share jar, a bag of clothes she outgrew, and a free Saturday morning. Her school is running a food drive, the shelter needs coats, and the food pantry needs helpers.
look.prompt: Match each thing Kim has to a place that could use it. Which gift costs no money at all?

check.q: Which of these is a way to share?
choices: Giving time at a food drive
check.why: Sharing can be money, things or time given to help someone else.

check.q: What should you do before giving money to someone who calls or messages you?
choices: Give quickly so you do not miss out
Ask them for your account number
Give only if they say it is urgent
check.why: Real groups never rush you, and a grown-up can check that the request is real.

check.q: What can a kid give to a food pantry?
choices: A can of food, or time sorting cans with a grown-up
check.why: Small gifts of food or time are real ways to help.

review.q: What does it mean to earn money?
choices: To get money for work you do
review.why: Earning is being paid for work.

review.q: Three lawns at $10 each, minus $4 for bags. What did you keep?
A $120 goal, saving $20 a week. How many weeks?
Why put savings in a jar with a picture instead of a pocket?
choices: You see the goal and the money does not get spent by accident
review.why: One place with a visible goal keeps the money on its job.

choices: Money put into a bank account
review.why: Deposits go in; withdrawals come out.

review.q: $100 saved at 2 percent for a year earns how much interest?
Income is $20. Save $8, share $2, snacks $4, bus $3, spending $3. Is the budget balanced?
Which order of filling the jars works best?
choices: Spend, then save what is left
Save first, then share, then spend
review.why: Filling save first makes sure saving actually happens.
